Commensal microbiota-coated biohybrid implants induce antibiofilm, osteogenic, and immunomodulatory responses in a human 3D immunocompetent model
Beyond Blood Cultures and Echocardiography: Emerging Diagnostics for Infective Endocarditis
abstract: Management of infective endocarditis (IE) is often confounded by the presence of prosthetic valves, transcatheter prostheses, and cardiovascular implantable electronic devices, as well as by changing epidemiologic risks and antimicrobial resistance patterns. For the diagnosis of IE, blood cultures and echocardiography remain foundational, but important gaps persist, particularly in culture-negative and prosthetic/device-associated infections. Contemporary diagnostic criteria and guidelines now support a multimodality approach incorporating molecular microbiology and advanced imaging. This review summarizes emerging technologies including broad-range 16S/18S/28S rRNA polymerase chain reaction and sequencing, fluorescence in situ hybridization coupled with sequencing, targeted and shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), plasma microbial cell-free DNA, cardiac computed tomography, and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography. We also examine the potential role of artificial intelligence in echocardiographic interpretation and of large language models in multimodal data integration. Current evidence suggests that tissue-based molecular testing generally provides greater microbiologic yield than valve culture in culture-negative IE, while blood-based mNGS and microbial cell-free DNA may extend pathogen detection after antibiotic exposure and reduce reliance on tissue-based diagnosis. However, heterogeneity in specimen handling, sequencing pipelines, contamination control, reporting thresholds, and clinical interpretation remains a major barrier to implementation. Future progress should move beyond pathogen detection toward rapid, reproducible, clinically actionable diagnosis that integrates organism identification, anatomic localization, disseminated disease, and personalized treatment. Prospective outcome trials, standardized workflows, cost-effectiveness studies, and multidisciplinary Endocarditis Team integration can help determine whether these technologies translate into better antimicrobial stewardship, procedural decision-making, and patient outcomes.

title: Gram-Negative Bacterial Resistance
abstract: The rapid worldwide spread of antimicrobial resistance among gram-negative bacteria is driven by a complex interplay of human, environmental, and health care-associated factors and accelerated by mobile genetic elements that facilitate the dissemination of resistance genes. Resistance in gram-negative bacteria arises primarily through reduced drug entry, active drug efflux, modification of antibiotic targets, and enzymatic drug inactivation, most notably through β-lactamase production. Clinically important resistant pathogens include extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales,with difficult-to-treat resistance, and carbapenem-resistant. Limited access to effective antibiotics and the continued emergence of resistance to available agents pose substantial challenges to the management of these infections. Appropriate management requires timely and accurate diagnostics, targeted use of newer β-lactam agents, effective source control, and judicious selection of treatment durations.

title: Bacteriophages versus priority pathogens: resistance mechanisms, therapeutic challenges, and opportunities for novel combinations
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a critical global health threat, and renewed interest in bacteriophage (phage) therapy highlights its potential as a targeted alternative to antibiotic monotherapy. However, phage resistance in bacteria remains a key limiting factor in phage therapy, driven by evolutionary adaptations to phage exposure. Antibacterial modalities (antibiotics, adjuvants, antimicrobial peptides, and RNA-based therapeutics) could help overcome these barriers and represent untapped potential for synergistic, precision antimicrobial interventions when combined with phage therapy. Importantly, bacterial physiology and environmental context could strongly influence treatment outcomes, underscoring the need for clinically relevant models for testing combinations. Integration of multi-omics and artificial intelligence-driven approaches could help predict patterns for the development of precision therapies and support the development of novel antimicrobial interventions.

title: Plague in the modern world: Ecological persistence, epidemic containment, and the limits of public health preparedness
abstract: Yersinia pestis persists across sylvatic rodent-flea reservoirs globally and is not currently amenable to eradication. Paleogenomic and paleoecological evidence indicates that historical plague pandemics reflected complex interactions among pathogen biology, environmental conditions, and societal vulnerabilities rather than pathogen virulence alone. Drawing a qualified epidemiological comparison to cholera, contemporary public health interventions show that effective disease control does not necessarily require eliminating a pathogen from its natural reservoirs; for plague, modern clinical and public health measures have substantially decoupled zoonotic spillovers from pandemic amplification. Whereas cholera control relies predominantly on water and sanitation barriers alongside clinical, vaccination, and surveillance programs, plague containment depends primarily on zoonotic monitoring, rapid diagnosis, early antimicrobial therapy, and contact management. The October 2026 unexplained fatal pneumonia in a Russian anti-plague laboratory worker illustrates both the capacity and the limitations of outbreak surveillance when targeted assays reported by national authorities are negative but etiology remains unresolved. With 97.7% of the 2646 confirmed human cases reported globally during 2019-2025 concentrated in two endemic countries, sustaining containment requires addressing healthcare inequities, maintaining clinical vigilance, monitoring antimicrobial resistance, and enforcing rigorous biosafety.

title: Shotgun Metagenomic Profiling of Phlebotomus papatasi (Diptera: Psychodidae, Phlebotomine) in Zoonotic Cutaneous Leishmaniasis Endemic Foci of Iraq: Microbiota, Resistome, and Virulome
abstract: This study aims to develop a regional baseline for future individual-level and comparative studies of microbial ecology and symbiont-based vector control. Phlebotomus papatasi is a major vector of Leishmania major and an important component of the transmission cycle of zoonotic cutaneous leishmaniasis (ZCL) in Iraq, although the internal microbial communities of this vector are poorly characterised in the region. In this study, shotgun metagenomic sequencing was employed to investigate the microbial communities of a pooled sample of 129 blood-fed female Ph. papatasi collected from ZCL-endemic foci in Nineveh Governorate, Iraq, from 2024 to 2025. Approximately 32.9 million raw reads were obtained from sequencing, with the quality-filtered, host-removed, and low-diversity-filtered reads analysed for taxonomic and functional profiles. The data revealed a complex microbial community inside blood-fed Ph. papatasi dominated by bacteria. Moreover, several species of Proteobacteria in blood-fed Ph. papatasi were detected, which accounted for 98.32% of the classified reads, with Enterobacter cloacae as the most common species (74.34% of classified reads). Strains associated with Wolbachia were also detected (approximately 8.96% of classified reads). The microbial data further revealed the presence of genes associated with antimicrobial resistance including oqxA/oqxB-associated efflux and AmpC-type β-lactamase families, and virulence factors associated with motility, iron acquisition, and secretion systems. Nevertheless, the data represented the distribution of sequencing reads within the pooled sample (single sample), rather than the prevalence or average abundance among individual sand flies.

title: In vitro activity of imipenem/relebactam against Enterobacterales isolates from China: results from the Study of Monitoring Antimicrobial Resistance Trends (SMART), 2020-2022
abstract: Imipenem/relebactam (IMR) is a β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combination that enhances the activity of imipenem against carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative pathogens by inhibiting class A and class C β-lactamases, particularly KPC. With the increasing prevalence of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) in China, evaluation of the in vitro activity of IMR is warranted. As part of the SMART surveillance program, Enterobacterales isolates were collected from 18 tertiary hospitals in China (2020-2022), including specimens from bloodstream, intra-abdominal, respiratory, and urinary tract infections (UTIs) in intensive care units (ICUs) and general wards. Species were identified by MALDI-TOF MS, and susceptibility was determined by broth microdilution. A total of 6182 Enterobacterales isolates were included, of which 19.1% were carbapenem-resistant. Higher rates of carbapenem resistance were observed among isolates from ICU patients and those causing urinary tract infections. IMR demonstrated substantially greater in vitro activity against CRKP than imipenem alone, resulting in a marked shift toward lower MIC distributions and an approximately fivefold reduction in the proportion of resistant isolates across both ICU and non-ICU settings. Compared with other β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations, IMR showed a higher proportion of isolates with MICs ≤1 mg/L and fewer isolates with elevated MICs than ceftazidime/avibactam or meropenem/vaborbactam, particularly among CRKP isolates. IMR exhibits in vitro activity against CRKP, particularly among isolates from ICU patients and those causing bloodstream infections. Our study suggests that IMR represents an important therapeutic option for infections caused by resistant Gram-negative pathogens, particularly carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales; however, further clinical data are needed to confirm efficacy.

title: Antimicrobial resistance and molecular characterization of extended-spectrum β-lactamase/AmpC β-lactamase-producing Proteus mirabilis isolates from companion dogs in South Korea (2018-2024)
abstract: To investigate antimicrobial resistance profiles and molecular characteristics of third-generation cephalosporin- and cephamycin-resistant Proteus mirabilis isolated from clinically ill dogs across South Korea from 2018 through 2024. Antimicrobial susceptibility of isolates was assessed by broth microdilution. Molecular characteristics were determined by polymerase chain reaction and multilocus sequence typing. In total, 667 P mirabilis were isolated from skin/ear, feces, and urine/reproductive systems of companion dogs. Among them, 27.3% of isolates exhibited a multidrug-resistant (MDR) phenotype. Molecular characterization of 38 extended-spectrum β-lactamase (5.7%)/AmpC β-lactamase-carrying strains revealed a high prevalence of β-lactamase cephamycinase-2 gene blaCMY-2 (65.8%) and β-lactamase cefotaximase gene blaCTX-M variants, including blaCTX-M-65, blaCTX-M-15, and blaCTX-M-90. Multilocus sequence typing identified 16 distinct sequence types (STs), with ST135 (39.5%) and ST212 (21.1%) emerging as the most prevalent lineages. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the first major cluster contains 31 isolates (81.6%) across 10 STs centered around ST135, whereas the second cluster comprises 7 isolates (18.4%) across 6 STs centered on ST292. Notably, the ST135-centered cluster was associated with robust MDR phenotypes. These findings indicate that companion dogs harboring MDR P mirabilis are among several potential reservoirs within the One Health context. Especially, clone ST135 may serve as a primary evolutionary axis and a high-risk endemic clone within the Korean canine population. Our study highlights the critical role of dominant lineages in dissemination of extended-spectrum β-lactamase/AmpC β-lactamase genes and emphasizes the urgent need for continuous One Health surveillance to monitor potential transmission of these clones between companion animals and humans.

title: Differential regulation of conjugative transfer and OMV-mediated ARG delivery by iprovalicarb and cycluron: Implications for pathway-specific risk assessment
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major driver of the rapid dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) among bacteria. Non-antibiotic compounds can promote plasmid-mediated conjugative transfer. In waterfowl farming, waterfowl frequently move among water, soil, and feces, which serve as reservoirs for pesticides and ARGs and thus potential hotspots for ARG spread. However, whether outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), an emerging ARG transmission pathway, are regulated by pesticides and respond in a manner consistent with conjugation is unclear. In this study, two pesticides detected in waterfowl farm environments, iprovalicarb and cycluron were selected to investigate their effects on conjugative transfer and OMV-mediated ARG dissemination. Both pesticides significantly promoted RP4 plasmid conjugation frequency at sub-inhibitory concentrations. This effect was associated with elevated bacterial reactive oxygen species (ROS), increased membrane permeability and fluidity, enhanced interbacterial contact, and altered energy metabolism. However, their effects on the OMV pathway diverged: iprovalicarb increased OMV production and vesicle size and was associated with more bla-positive colonies after OMV exposure, whereas cycluron inhibited OMV production. This decoupling suggests that pesticides can differentially regulate conjugative and OMV-mediated ARG transfer. However, the bla gene was not stably inherited in recipient bacteria. Overall, these findings highlight the need to evaluate these two pathways separately when assessing the risk of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Analytical instability and aqueous degradation of carbapenem antibiotics: formation of β-lactam-retaining transformation products
authors: Martinez I Quer A et al.
abstract: Carbapenems are last-resort antibiotics used to treat severe infections caused by multidrug-resistant bacteria. Despite their clinical importance and documented consumption, they remain largely undetected in environmental monitoring studies. This study investigated whether the lack of detection of carbapenems in environmental studies reflects analytical limitations, rapid degradation, or both. Sensitive LC-MS/MS methods were developed for selected carbapenems and used to assess compound stability under analytical and environmentally relevant conditions. All investigated carbapenems exhibited limited stability, with degradation strongly accelerated by methanol. Under environmentally relevant conditions, parent compounds degraded rapidly in river water, biofilm-containing water, and UV-exposed water, with little difference between treatments. High-resolution LC-MS/MS analysis revealed formation of multiple transformation products (TPs) retaining an intact β-lactam ring. Meropenem generated four β-lactam-retaining TPs, and faropenem generated four, several of which remained detectable long after disappearance of the parent compounds. These findings help explain the lack of detection of carbapenems in environmental surveys and demonstrate that disappearance of parent compounds does not necessarily imply elimination of β-lactam-containing structures. The persistence of β-lactam-retaining TPs suggests that environmental exposure and associated selective pressure may persist after parent carbapenems have degraded, highlighting the need for further investigation of their biological activity and potential role in antimicrobial resistance.

title: Bioinformatics for Healthcare Quality Management: Clinical Outcomes, Implementation Barriers, and Care Improvement
abstract: The bioinformatics-enabled workflows as quality-management tools have become central to modern healthcare, enabling genomic sequencing, transcriptomics, proteomics, and multiomics integration to support clinical decision-making. Despite expanding adoption, synthesized evidence on measurable clinical value and organizational, workforce, interoperability, governance, and equity barriers remains limited. To synthesize evidence on the contribution of bioinformatics-enabled workflows to healthcare quality improvement, care-process performance, clinical decision-making, patient outcomes, and implementation challenges from 2015 to 2025. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore. We included studies from real-world healthcare or public health settings where bioinformatics supported diagnostic quality, timeliness, treatment appropriateness, patient safety, and workflow efficiency, or operational decision-making, reporting quantitative outcomes including diagnostic yield, time-to-diagnosis, treatment modification, or economic impact. Twenty studies met the selection criteria, spanning precision oncology, pharmacogenomics, infectious disease surveillance, clinical genomics and rare disease diagnosis, and multiomics biomarker translation. Across these domains, bioinformatics-enabled workflows improved diagnostic yield (25%-40% in rare disease genomics) and diagnostic accuracy, and shortened time-to-diagnosis, from 4-6 weeks to as little as 3 days in acute pediatric care and from weeks to under 24 hours for pathogen genomic surveillance. Workflows also supported treatment modification, with matched or altered therapy in 33%-37% of oncology cases, and improved pathogen detection and antimicrobial-resistance monitoring. Economic evidence, although still limited, was favorable: first-line exome sequencing was cost-saving, with average reductions of approximately US$9000 per patient in rare disease diagnosis. Although precision medicine relies heavily on bioinformatics, improvements to infrastructure, consistent governance, and capacity building for clinical staff are essential to ensure its scalable and equitable implementation.

title: Phage-encoded PciP differentially regulates Pseudomonas aeruginosa swarming motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms
abstract: is an opportunistic pathogen whose intrinsic antibiotic resistance and complex virulence regulatory networks pose major clinical challenges. Bacteriophages and their encoded proteins have emerged as potential modulators of bacterial physiology, yet the mechanisms by which phage proteins influence bacterial virulence remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified PciP, an early protein encoded by the lytic phage PAYQ66, which suppresses pyocyanin production and swarming motility in. PciP reduces PQS levels and suppresses quorum-sensing gene transcription. PciP associates with CheV, and genetic analysis indicates that CheV is required for the PciP-mediated inhibition of swarming but not for the PciP-mediated suppression of PQS and pyocyanin production. Expression of PciP attenuates virulence in infection models. Together, these findings reveal that PciP differentially modulates swarming motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms. These results provide mechanistic insights into how a phage-encoded protein reprograms host regulatory networks.IMPORTANCEis a major opportunistic pathogen that is increasingly difficult to treat due to intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance. Bacteriophages encode diverse proteins that can interfere with bacterial regulatory networks, yet many remain functionally uncharacterized. Here, we characterize PciP, a protein encoded by the lytic phage PAYQ66, and show that it modulates bacterial motility and quorum-sensing-associated phenotypes through distinct mechanisms. PciP associates with CheV and inhibits swarming motility in a CheV-dependent manner, whereas PciP-mediated suppression of PQS and pyocyanin production persists in the absence of CheV. These combined effects significantly reduce pathogenicity in both animal and plant infection models. This study advances our understanding of phage-host interactions by demonstrating that a phage-encoded protein can differentially modulate host regulatory outputs via CheV-dependent and CheV-independent mechanisms.

title: Impact of ESKAPE pathogens on the One Health framework considering epidemiology and environmental occurrence
abstract: SUMMARYThe ESKAPE group of pathogens represents one of the most critical threats to global health due to their capacity to evade antimicrobial treatments. This review provides a structured synthesis of the literature addressing antimicrobial resistance mechanisms, epidemiological relevance, clinical impact, and emerging strategies for containment within a One Health framework. Relevant studies and surveillance reports were analyzed to characterize the global distribution and burden of these organisms across human, animal, and environmental settings. The evidence indicates that ESKAPE pathogens remain leading causes of healthcare-associated infections while increasingly being identified in non-clinical reservoirs, highlighting the interconnected nature of antimicrobial resistance. Recent findings point to sustained high morbidity and mortality associated with these pathogens, driven by the expansion of multidrug-resistant lineages, and the limited effectiveness of current therapeutic options. Key challenges identified include gaps in surveillance integration, the spread of resistance determinants across sectors, and variability in infection control practices. Addressing these issues requires coordinated strategies that integrate surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention, and the development of novel therapeutics within a comprehensive One Health approach.

title: Comparative analysis of various infection models to provide methodological insights for the characterization of new antivirulence drugs to fight antibioresistance
abstract: Bacterial infections remain a major global health burden, amplified by the rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Among priority pathogens, the ESKAPEE group represents a critical threat due to their high prevalence in healthcare-associated infections, and their capacity to acquire multidrug resistance. Antivirulence strategies, aiming at disarming pathogens rather than inhibiting their growth, constitute a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics. Their development, however, is hindered by the lack of suitable experimental models to evaluate virulence and antivirulence efficacy. Here, we establish complementaryandinfection models to characterize pathogenicity and assess antivirulence activity against clinically relevant ESKAPEE bacteria (). We developed a robust nitric oxide (NO)-basedassay that mimics host immune nitrosative stress and enables quantitative evaluation of bacterial resistance to innate immune defenses. In parallel, we established comparative insect infection models usingandspecies, allowing reproducible assessment of bacterial virulence across multiple hosts and pathogens. These models highlighted marked differences in pathogenic potential depending on both bacterial species and host background. As a proof of concept, we applied these systems to characterize NM102, a first-in-class antivirulence compound targeting the DNA repair protein Mfd. NM102 significantly reduced bacterial survival under NO stressand decreased bacterial burdenin insect infection models. Together, our results demonstrate that combining immune-mimickingassays with complementary insect models provides a powerful and ethically acceptable platform to study bacterial pathogenicity and to accelerate the development of innovative antivirulence therapeutics to combat AMR.IMPORTANCEBacterial infections remain a major public health challenge, worsened by the rapid rise of antimicrobial resistance. Among the most concerning pathogens are the ESKAPEE bacteria, which frequently cause hospital-acquired infections and are often resistant to multiple antibiotics. Antivirulence strategies offer promising alternatives to traditional treatments by disarming bacteria rather than killing them, potentially reducing the risk of resistance. However, progress in this field has been limited by the lack of reliable models to measure bacterial virulence and evaluate antivirulence compounds. In this study, we developed complementary models to better assess bacterial pathogenicity and treatment efficacy. We created anassay that mimics immune defenses and established insect infection models to compare virulence across pathogens and hosts. Using these systems, we tested NM102, a first-in-class antivirulence compound targeting bacterial DNA repair. NM102 reduced bacterial survival and infection severity, highlighting the potential of antivirulence approaches as innovative therapies against drug-resistant infections.

title: The global landscape of Campylobacter: genomic epidemiology, AMR trends, and the path to vaccine development
abstract: species, particularlyand, are leading causes of bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide, responsible for an estimated 500 million cases of acute diarrheal illness annually. Despite their global prevalence and association with severe post-infectious sequelae such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, no licensed vaccine exists, and the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance further complicates clinical management. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the epidemiology, genomic diversity, antimicrobial resistance mechanisms, and vaccine development strategies forspecies, with emphasis on global trends and public health relevance in the United States. Through a One Health lens, we examine transmission across human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, and highlight the role of integrated genomic surveillance in tracking clonal expansion, horizontal gene transfer, and resistance dissemination. We also examine historical and current approaches to vaccine development, including whole-cell, subunit, glycoconjugate, and genomics-guided antigen discovery strategies. Challenges such as antigenic variability, phase variation, and inadequate experimental models have impeded progress, though recent genomics-informed interventions show promise in both poultry and human contexts. Continued investment in genomic surveillance, antimicrobial resistance, and rational antigen selection will be essential for developing effective vaccines and reducing the global burden of campylobacteriosis.

title: A putative GtrB-like glycosyltransferase modulates cation-dependent BCP8-2 phage infection and cell surface structure in Bacillus cereus
abstract: is a foodborne pathogen of growing concern due to its persistence and antimicrobial resistance. To identify host determinants influencing susceptibility to phage BCP8-2, a mini-Tntransposon mutant library ofATCC 14579 was constructed and screened for altered phage susceptibility. A mutant (BC2012) showing partial resistance carried an insertion in(previously), encoding a putative GtrB-like bactoprenol glycosyltransferase. Complementation restored phage sensitivity, confirming its functional involvement. The mutant showed a slight reduction in efficiency of plating, whereas, adsorption assay revealed significantly reduced phage binding and infectivity, particularly under cation-rich conditions. Furthermore, adsorption kinetics and one-step growth curve in mutant supported thatmutation affects initial adsorption. Microscopy showed altered surface morphology with thinner, smoother cell walls. These data indicate thataffects surface properties essential for cation-dependent phage adsorption and infection and provide a foundation for future studies on the role of surface glycosylation and ionic interactions in Gram-positive phage biology.IMPORTANCEPathogenicis resilient across diverse environments and produces diverse toxins linked to foodborne outbreaks. Bacteriophages provide an effective strategy to control; however, molecular targets of phage-host interaction are poorly understood, limiting the effective phage-based control. The current study addresses this gap by identifying a putative bactoprenol glycosyltransferase (GtrB), a viral factor in phage BCP8-2 susceptibility. Data obtained highlight a partial reduction of phage infection in themutant, demonstrating that GtrB-like glycosyltransferase significantly contributes to BCP8-2 phage infection and adsorption. Our findings provide significant insights into advancing phage therapy, antibiotic resistance, andbiocontrol in food and clinical settings.

title: Bacterial Surfaces and Barriers: Biogenesis and Pathogen-Host Interactions
abstract: The bacterial surface represents the primary interface between pathogens and hosts, yet its chemical and architectural complexity challenges conventional classification. This Review examines structural organization, molecular composition, and biogenesis of bacterial surface components across the Gracilicutes and Terrabacteria clades, linking mechanistic detail to pathogenic function. We describe lipid diversity, integral membrane protein biogenesis, and lipoprotein processing at the inner membrane and how these components support surface remodeling, secretion, and virulence. We then examine the peptidoglycan layer and its role in immune recognition and surface protein display, teichoic acids and their contributions to antimicrobial resistance and immune evasion, and S layers, whose crystalline arrays mediate adhesion and immune modulation. The outer membrane section covers lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, outer membrane protein biogenesis and folding, lipoprotein trafficking, and contributions to pathogenicity, while the mycobacterial section addresses the mycolyl-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan complex and virulence factors. We discuss bacterial capsule diversity, biosynthesis, and use as vaccine antigens, along with adhesive surface structures such as fimbriae, pili, and curli fibers and their roles in colonization and biofilm formation, before covering secretion systems types I through XI and their contributions to virulence. This Review provides a framework for understanding how bacterial surface diversity shapes infection and identifies chemical vulnerabilities for therapeutics.

title: Exploring Barriers, Facilitators, and Strategies for the Etiological Management of Sexually Transmitted Infections in Brazil: A Qualitative Study Using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR)
abstract: In Brazil, syndromic management remains the standard approach for male urethral discharge despite the growing need for etiological diagnosis. This study explored barriers, facilitators, and implementation strategies for adopting the etiological approach using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). A qualitative study was conducted through semi-structured online interviews with health professionals. Interview transcripts were analyzed deductively using the CFIR Codebook and inductively to identify emerging themes. From March to April 2023, 15 professionals from all Brazilian regions were interviewed: five clinicians, five laboratory professionals, and five public health managers. Major barriers for implementing the etiological approach included limited systematic epidemiological data, the absence of rapid immunochromatographic STI tests, limited workforce capacity, and high staff turnover. Key facilitators were timely diagnosis and treatment of asymptomatic infections, targeted therapy based on pathogen identification, and antimicrobial resistance surveillance through biological sample collection. Proposed strategies involved phased introduction, with both approaches initially coexisting: syndromic treatment for symptomatic cases with sample collection to identify the causative agent, discussion of results during follow-up consultations, and screening of asymptomatic cases. Additionally, interviewees recommended mandatory STI notification for standardized data generation, awareness raising, and public policy planning. They also emphasized the need for national meetings on STIs beyond syphilis, HIV, and viral hepatitis. Although the syndromic approach remains necessary in Brazil, health professionals demonstrated readiness to implement the etiological approach and identified practical strategies to support its integration into STI prevention and control programs.

title: Type IV-Dominated Plasmid-Encoded CRISPR-Cas Systems Are Enriched in Multireplicon and Multi-Stressor Resistance Plasmids Across the Global Plasmidome
abstract: Plasmids are central vectors of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). However, the features that distinguish the most epidemiologically successful resistance plasmids remain incompletely understood. CRISPR-Cas systems are classically regarded as barriers to horizontal gene transfer, which makes their occurrence within resistance plasmids yet unexplored at large scale. Here we analyzed 72,555 curated plasmid sequences from the Plasmid database (PLSDB) to test whether plasmid-encoded CRISPR-Cas systems are non-randomly associated with plasmid architecture and multi-stressor resistance across a large scale plasmidome. Using a three-tier classification of CRISPR-Cas system integrity based on array quality and Cas gene presence, we found that intact systems, defined by the co-occurrence of a high-confidence array and cas genes within the same replicon, were rare (1.03%) but strongly and specifically enriched in multireplicon plasmids (OR = 12.36) and in plasmids resistant to multiple stressor classes (MSR; OR = 6.25). These associations were robust to clonal redundancy: after dereplicating near-identical sequences over 100 iterations, both remained significant in every iteration, whereas the association with antimicrobial multidrug resistance (MDR) collapsed, identifying it as an artifact of clonal expansion. Intact systems were concentrated in high-risk IncF and IncH backbones and were more prevalent in plasmids from environmental sources than in those from clinical sources. Type IV-A was the predominant subtype (38.8% of intact systems), consistent with its near-exclusive association with mobile genetic elements and its proposed role in inter-plasmid competition rather than host defense. Together, these findings suggest that plasmid-encoded CRISPR-Cas systems, whether retaining defense-associated functions or acting as intra-MGE competition elements, are non-randomly retained in structurally complex, multi-stressor plasmid backbones that are particularly effective at accumulating and disseminating antimicrobial resistance.

title: Extensively Drug-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa Keratitis After Photorefractive Keratectomy Because of Contaminated Eye Drops: Experience With Colistin-Based Therapy
abstract: This study aims to report the clinico-microbiological characteristics of cases of infectious keratitis caused by extensively drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa after photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) and to identify the source of infection. Retrospective review of 7 eyes from 4 patients presenting with infectious keratitis after bilateral PRK performed at different centers and time points, evaluated at a tertiary eye care center in India between March 2024 and August 2025. We analyzed demographic, clinical, microbiological, treatment, and outcome data. The study included 7 eyes from 4 patients. Patients presented, on average, after 2.5 days (range, 1-4 ), and visual acuity ranged from 20/50 to perception of light with inaccurate projection of rays. Corneal infiltrates were central and full-thickness, with severe stromal lysis in 5 of the 7 eyes; 1 eye had a midstromal infiltrate, and 1 eye had pinpoint anterior stromal infiltrates. Hypopyon was present in 6 eyes. In all cases, microbiological examination revealed Gram-negative bacilli, confirmed to be Pseudomonas aeruginosa on culture. The isolate was resistant to all antibiotic classes, with intermediate susceptibility only to colistin. Six of 7 eyes recovered with medical therapy (topical colistin 0.19%) alone, whereas 1 eye underwent therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty (TPK). Source evaluation in all cases revealed identical organisms with similar antimicrobial resistance patterns in the eye drops used and left over by the patient, and in unopened similar drops. This series highlights early recognition of extensively drug-resistant infections after PRK surgery, source identification, and prompt, microbiology-guided therapy, resulting in favorable outcomes.

title: Marker-Free Chromosomal Integration of a Multigene Cassette in Escherichia coli for Heavy-Metal Bioremediation Development
abstract: Heavy metal contamination remains a significant environmental challenge due to the persistence, toxicity, and bioaccumulation of metal pollutants. Genetically engineered bacteria offer a potential approach to heavy metal remediation; however, plasmid-based expression systems can present limitations associated with plasmid maintenance and antibiotic selection. This study describes a protocol for constructing a marker-free, multigene recombinant E. coli strain designed for the chromosomal integration of genes associated with heavy-metal resistance and sequestration. A 4,741 bp multigene cassette comprising cadD, cadA, and metallothionein (mt), together with a lipoprotein outer membrane protein A (Lpp-OmpA) surface display system and a green fluorescent protein (gfp) reporter gene under the control of the constitutive pyruvate dehydrogenase (Ppdh) promoter, was designed and synthesized. The construct was cloned into the pKIKOArsBKm integration vector and introduced into E. coli MG1655 using lambda (λ) Red-mediated recombination. The kanamycin resistance cassette was subsequently excised using the flippase-flippase recognition target (FLP-FRT) recombination system. Construct assembly and chromosomal integration were evaluated by restriction enzyme analysis, plasmid isolation, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification, while loss of antibiotic resistance was assessed by antibiotic sensitivity testing. Amplification of the expected cadD, cadA, and mt fragments from genomic DNA, together with the absence of detectable plasmid DNA, provided evidence consistent with chromosomal integration of the multigene cassette. Although this protocol establishes a framework for constructing and molecularly evaluating the recombinant strain, definitive confirmation of the integration locus, functional gene expression, long-term genetic stability, and heavy metal biosorption performance requires further experimental validation.

title: Regarding: European genomic: An untapped opportunity to strengthen the fight against antimicrobial resistance
Syphilis: clinical, diagnostic and therapeutic update
abstract: Syphilis remains a major global public health concern due to the sustained increase in incidence observed over recent decades, particularly among high-risk populations. Its broad clinical spectrum and ability to mimic numerous dermatological and systemic diseases continue to make it a relevant diagnostic challenge in dermatological practice. This review summarizes the main epidemiological, microbiological, clinical, diagnostic, and therapeutic aspects of Treponema pallidum infection, with special emphasis on mucocutaneous manifestations and recent advances in molecular diagnostic techniques. Current therapeutic strategies, clinical and serological follow-up, and special situations such as neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, pregnancy, and HIV infection are also reviewed. Finally, emerging preventive challenges are discussed, including doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (DoxyPEP), antimicrobial resistance, and future perspectives in vaccine development.

title: Fe/Mn oxide-loaded biochars mitigate antibiotic resistance gene pollution and dissemination potential in agricultural soils
abstract: Spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in agricultural soils threatens ecological and public health. Functionalized biochars hold promise for remediating biological contaminants, yet the performance of Fe/Mn oxide-loaded biochars (Fe/Mn-MBCs) in mitigating soil ARG pollution remains unclear. Herein, we investigated the effects and mechanisms of Fe/Mn-MBCs prepared via one-pot pyrolysis of pig manure impregnated with ferric nitrate and potassium permanganate on ARG abundance and risk using soil microcosms combined with bacterial conjugation and natural transformation assays. While pristine biochar increased total ARG relative abundance, Fe/Mn-MBCs bearing nano-sized oxides (e.g., FeO, MnO, MnO) decreased it by 23.17%-44.54%, and high-risk ARGs (aadE, floR) by 28.73%-50.19%, demonstrating the feasibility for mitigating soil ARG pollution and health risks. Mechanistically, Fe/Mn-MBCs reshaped the bacterial community by enriching Fe/Mn-redox bacteria (e.g., Terrimonas, Stenotrophobacter), while strengthening dispersal limitation of potential ARG hosts (e.g., Actinobacteria, Firmicutes). Fe/Mn-MBCs also suppressed horizontal gene transfer (HGT), as evidenced by the decreased abundances of mobile genetic elements (intI1, tn916, tnpA) by 10.60%-40.80%. This was further confirmed by the decreased frequencies of conjugation and transformation. Fe/Mn-MBCs suppressed intracellular ARG conjugations by reducing cell membrane permeability, ATP synthesis, and bacterial motility, while inhibiting extracellular ARGs (eARGs) transformation via plasmid adsorption and reduced eARG availability. These findings advance mechanistic understanding of Fe/Mn-MBCs in mitigating soil ARG pollution through potential ARG host reduction and HGT suppression, and guide the rational design of functionalized biochars as an in‑situ remediation strategy against antimicrobial resistance in agroecosystems.

title: Genomic Investigation of a Carbapenem-Resistant Chromobacterium haemolyticum Cluster Reveals Environmental Introduction and Nosocomial Transmission
abstract: To investigate the source and transmission dynamics of a cluster of four Chromobacterium haemolyticum infections in an intensive care unit (ICU) and to characterize their antimicrobial resistance profiles. An epidemiological investigation was conducted involving four ICU patients identified between July 2024 and August 2025. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on eight isolates, and core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism (cgSNP) analysis was used to assess their genetic relatedness. Antimicrobial resistance genes were identified using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), while resistance-associated point mutations were detected using AMRFinderPlus. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was constructed based on 26 genomes to investigate the genomic relationships among the isolates. Two distinct epidemiological events were identified. Three patients harbored closely related isolates forming a clonal cluster with 0-10 SNP differences, linked to an index case with a history of near-drowning. In contrast, an isolate recovered from a patient with independent environmental exposure was genetically unrelated to the cluster, differing by >38,000 SNPs. All cluster isolates carried the chromosomal blagene, encoding a class A carbapenemase related to Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC), and displayed carbapenem resistance, unlike previously reported carbapenem-susceptible C. haemolyticum strains. Transmission ceased during the winter, with Patient 2 serving as a potential long-term reservoir. This study provides the first genomic evidence supporting nosocomial transmission of C. haemolyticum. The concordant resistance profiles observed in the outbreak and unrelated isolates suggest that blamay be a key determinant of carbapenem resistance in C. haemolyticum, challenging the assumption that empirical carbapenem therapy is reliably effective against this pathogen.

title: Licorice and fermented licorice extracts alleviate Mycoplasma gallisepticum infection through modulation of the DC-SIGN/Wnt/β-catenin signaling axis
abstract: Mycoplasma gallisepticum (MG) is the principal etiological agent of chronic respiratory disease (CRD) in chickens, compromising poultry performance and causing substantial economic losses. Conventional antibiotic therapy is constrained by antimicrobial resistance and drug-residue concerns, creating an urgent need for safe, effective, and environmentally friendly alternatives. Here, we report the first systematic investigation of the molecular mechanism and translational potential of Licorice extract (Let) and its Fermented Licorice extract (FLet) in suppressing MG infection via modulation of the DC-SIGN/WNT signaling axis. In vitro, FLet exhibited stronger growth-inhibitory activity against MG than Let, while Let and FLet showed no detectable cytotoxicity toward HD11 cells within the tested concentration range of 0.02-4 mg/mL.In MG-infected HD11 cells, both Let and FLet reduced the expression of the MG adhesion-associated factor GapA and decreased MG genomic load. In parallel, Let and FLet modulated MG-induced inflammatory responses, as evidenced by decreased TNF-α and IL-1β and increased IL-4 and IL-10 levels, and alleviated MG-induced apoptosis by downregulating Caspase-3 and Bax while upregulating Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL. In vivo, licorice extract or fermented preparation improved body-weight gain and alleviated splenic lesions in MG-infected chickens, and reduced inflammatory and apoptosis-related markers in spleen. Therapeutic efficacy did not differ significantly from tiamulin (p > 0.05). Mechanistic analyses showed that Let and FLet treatment was associated with reduced DC-SIGN expression and changes in Wnt/β-catenin pathway-related molecules.. DC-SIGN knockdown reduced expression of β-catenin and c-Myc, supporting a regulatory role of DC-SIGN over WNT signaling. Collectively, Let and FLet reduced GapA expression and MG genomic load, attenuated cytokine dysregulation, and decreased apoptosis in HD11 cells. In MG-challenged chickens, Let and FLet improved body-weight gain and alleviated splenic lesions. For the evaluated outcomes, no significant differences were detected between the Let/FLet-treated groups and the tiamulin-treated group under the present experimental conditions. These effects were accompanied by reduced DC-SIGN expression and modulation of Wnt/β-catenin pathway-related molecules.

title: Occurrence and antimicrobial resistance of Acinetobacter baumannii in cats, veterinary hospital environments and medical wastes in Bangladesh
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii presence in veterinary hospitals and companion animals is still poorly investigated despite its significance. The present study aimed to investigate the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and resistance genes of A. baumannii in cats, veterinary hospital environments, and veterinary medical wastes in Bangladesh. Samples were collected from oral, rectal, and wound swabs of cats (n = 100) attending ten veterinary hospitals, as well as from environmental surfaces (n = 111) and wastes (n = 61) generated within these facilities. Isolates were identified by PCR targeting 16S rRNA (genus) and bla(species) genes; antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion and broth microdilution following CLSI standards, and resistance genes (bla, bla) were screened by PCR. A high prevalence of A. baumannii was observed in cats (37%), while 26.1% in environmental samples and 21.3% in waste samples. Apparently sick cats had significantly higher prevalence (p = 0.049) than apparently healthy cats. All isolates were imipenem resistant, consistent with carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB). High resistance was also observed against cefotaxime and ceftriaxone. Multidrug resistance (MDR) was detected in 26.7%, 37.9%, and 30.8% of isolates from cats, environmental, and waste sources, respectively. The blagene was detected in only two cat isolates, whereas blawas identified in one cat isolate and one environmental isolate. In conclusion, these findings identify cats, which live in close proximity to humans, as a possible CRAB reservoir, and veterinary hospital environments and waste as potential sources of persistence and dissemination, raising concern for zoonotic spread and underscoring occupational and public health risk.

title: Spatial metabolic insights of Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm treatments using stable isotope labeling with DESI mass spectrometry imaging
abstract: Bacteria form biofilms on diverse substrates, and these communities can cause persistent infections owing to their elevated antibiotic resistance. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major cause of chronic infections because of its ability to form biofilms, which makes it difficult to eradicate with conventional antibiotics. The metabolic response of P. aeruginosa biofilms to antibiotic treatment, however, remains only partially understood. Here, desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry imaging (DESI-MSI) was used to map the spatial metabolic responses of mature and developing P. aeruginosa biofilms to ciprofloxacin and two ciprofloxacin-nitroxide hybrids. Stable isotope labeling of metabolites was used to support the spatial interpretation of quorum-sensing (QS) metabolites within the chemically complex and dynamic spatial environment of biofilms and to understand their biosynthetic pathway. Ciprofloxacin induced localized metabolic changes and selective reorganization of quorum-sensing and redox-associated metabolites in biofilms. Both hybrids underwent heterogeneous in situ reduction to their inactive hydroxylamine forms within biofilms. These results indicate that DESI-MSI with stable isotope labeling can resolve growth-stage-dependent colony biofilm metabolism and characterize the metabolic response of biofilms to antibiotic treatment.

title: Conjugative Transfer Potential of Antibiotic Resistance from Wastewater-derived Coliforms to riverine Escherichia coli
abstract: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) discharged into rivers from wastewater treatment plants disseminate antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) through conjugative transfer, suggesting that aquatic environments serve as reservoirs for spreading antibiotic resistance. However, the actual extent of such dissemination of antibiotic resistance is unclear. This study investigated changes in the microbiota and antibiotic resistance profiles of other coliforms during the wastewater treatment process and evaluated whether other antibiotic-resistant coliforms persisting in treated wastewater could potentially transfer antibiotic resistance to Escherichia coli in receiving waters. The treatment process substantially reduced, but did not eliminate, E. coli and other coliforms (most probable number [MPN]/100 mL = 5 for E. coli and 4.3 × 10² for other coliforms), which were subsequently discharged into rivers. The resistance rates of other coliforms tended to increase throughout the treatment process, and the proportion of multidrug-resistant bacteria increased (influent: 4.9%, biologically treated water: 4.3%, effluent: 15.8%). Conjugation experiments using the filter mating method revealed the transfer of ARGs from Klebsiella species to E. coli (conjugation frequency: 10-10), suggesting the potential for antibiotic resistance transfer within biofilms. Experiments under simplified riverbed biofilm conditions confirmed the transfer of rifampicin resistance genes introduced into E. coli to antibiotic-resistant other coliforms (conjugation frequency: 9.7 × 10-5.3 × 10). The abundance of antibiotic-resistant other coliforms in the biofilm was 5.08 × 10² MPN/mL, which was lower than the observed conjugation frequencies, suggesting that the discharge area of treated wastewater is unlikely to function as a significant hotspot for ARB dissemination.

title: Pretrained graph transformer-driven de novo design and machine learning prioritization of computationally predicted ENR-InhA (InhA) inhibitors with potential relevance to drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abstract: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) undermines frontline therapy, and conventional drug discovery is slow and resource intensive. We present an integrated computational pipeline for the de novo design of inhibitors of a single clinically validated target, the NADH-dependent enoyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] reductase of(ENR-InhA, encoded by). Bioactive compounds were retrieved from ChEMBL and curated to 80 with equality-qualified ICvalues. Four conventional machine-learning models and one deep neural network were trained on Morgan and MACCS fingerprints to predict pIC. DrugGEN, a pretrained graph-transformer generative adversarial network, designed de novo molecules. Of 74 generated, 67 were novel relative to the curated set (nearest-neighbour Tanimoto < 0.85), and the 23 with predicted pIC ≥ 7.0 proceeded to ADMET screening and docking. Three compounds met all drug-likeness criteria, raised no toxicity alerts in the models applied, and gave docking scores (-8.27, -7.66, and -7.76 kcal/mol) more negative than direct ENR-InhA inhibitors docked identically. All three complexes maintained stable RMSD profiles over 200 ns of molecular dynamics, and compound 3 showed the greatest rigidity and broadest interaction profile. These are computationally prioritized candidates of potential relevance to drug-resistant tuberculosis; none was tested againstor drug-resistant isolates.

title: Chiral Gold Nanohedgehogs With Stereocomplementary Synergy for Potent Antibacterial Activity
abstract: This study developed an active, highly efficient physical antibacterial strategy that exploits chiral nanomaterials to effectively recognize and interact with the chiral microenvironment of bacterial membranes. Chiral gold nanohedgehogs (L/D-Au NH) are designed and fabricated with a unique morphology that facilitates "stereospecific matching" to bacterial membranes. Experimental results demonstrate that D-Au NH exhibit a remarkable 43.7% improvement in mechanical antibacterial activity compared to their L-Au NH counterparts. This finding quantitatively substantiates the rational chiral configuration for the antibacterial properties, which can be attributed to the enhanced bacterial recognition and stronger interfacial interactions with chiral components present on bacterial cell membranes, as indicated by the remarkable surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) signal amplification observed for lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and peptidoglycan (PG). Furthermore, these chiral nanostructures exhibit superior photothermal conversion efficiency upon activation with chirality-matched circularly polarized light (CPL), thereby synergistically enhancing antibacterial efficacy. Consequently, the developed D-Au NH enable the almost complete eradication of bacterial biofilms. This research underscores the considerable biomedical potential of precisely engineered chiral nanomaterials in combating antibiotic resistance.

title: PBP1A and LdtJ transpeptidase activities are crucial for cell envelope homeostasis and counteract the selection of colistin resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii
abstract: The multilayered cell envelope ofis an essential structure that maintains cellular integrity and protects the bacterial cell against external stresses and antibiotics. It consists of an inner membrane, a thin peptidoglycan (PG) layer, and an asymmetric outer membrane (OM) enriched in lipooligosaccharide (LOS), whose lipid A moiety is the target of colistin, a last-resort antibiotic. Although lipid A is essential in most Gram-negative bacteria,can survive without LOS through envelope remodeling, particularly in strains producing low levels of the bifunctional penicillin-binding protein PBP1A (encoded by) or in Δmutants. Here, we identify a genetic and functional interplay between the LD-transpeptidase LdtJ, which generates 3-3 cross-links, and PBP1A, which catalyzes 4-3 transpeptidation during PG synthesis. We show that simultaneous inactivation of both enzymes severely affects growth, viable counts, morphology, and OM homeostasis. PG analyses revealed that the ΔΔmutants display reduced overall cross-linking and shorter glycan chains, consistent with a weakened sacculus. Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated that PBP1A associates with LdtJ, suggesting that the two proteins may act in close proximity during PG synthesis. Notably, ΔΔmutants exhibited the highest recovery frequency of colistin-resistant, LOS-deficient variants compared with wild type or single mutants. Together, our findings indicate that 4-3 and 3-3 transpeptidase activities play complementary roles in PG synthesis and remodeling, contributing to envelope stability in, and that disruption of these activities favors the emergence of colistin resistance. This work further highlights the importance of PG remodeling in maintaining envelope homeostasis and suggests that proper PG cross-linking acts as a physiological constraint to limit the emergence of LOS-deficient colistin-resistant variants in, providing new insight into mechanisms that contribute to envelope destabilization.IMPORTANCEThe global rise of multidrug-resistantrepresents an urgent clinical threat, driven by its capacity to withstand cell envelope damage and escape last-resort antibiotics such as colistin. Although peptidoglycan synthesis and remodeling are known to influence outer membrane stability, how these processes interact inremains unclear. Here, we identify genetic and functional interactions between two major peptidoglycan biosynthetic and remodeling activities, 4-3 and 3-3 transpeptidation, mediated by the bifunctional PBP1A and the LD-transpeptidase LdtJ, respectively. Disrupting these activities weakens the peptidoglycan, destabilizes the outer membrane, and increases the emergence of lipooligosaccharide-deficient, colistin-resistant variants. These findings highlight the importance of proper peptidoglycan cross-linking for envelope homeostasis inand provide insight into how disruptions in peptidoglycan architecture influence antibiotic resistance.

title: Sleeper agents: asymptomatic Acinetobacter colonization and underlying mechanisms
abstract: and otherspecies are a growing public health concern because they commonly cause healthcare-associated infections.spp. are often multi-drug resistant, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, understanding the reservoirs forspp. in healthcare settings is particularly important to infection control.spp. are known to asymptomatically colonize the human gut, skin, and respiratory flora, and recent work has found the prevalence ofcolonization is high in patients in healthcare environments, such as hospitals and long-term care facilities. Patients colonized byare at increased risk of developing clinical infections, including by the same strains. Additionally, multiple studies report transmission ofstrains to other patients in the same healthcare setting. Recent mechanistic studies ongut colonization have found that the microbiota, host immunity, and diet contribute to colonization resistance in animal models. Here, we review the epidemiologic evidence for asymptomatic colonization as a clinically important reservoir forand examine the nascent study of the molecular mechanisms ofcolonization. We discuss future prospects for understandingcolonization that may help develop strategies to support colonization resistance and prevent infections.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Molecular Epidemiology of Haemophilus influenzae Causing Pediatric Acute Otitis Media in Japan
abstract: Antimicrobial-resistant strains of Haemophilus influenzae are associated with treatment failure and recurrence in acute otitis media (AOM). We aimed to characterize the current antimicrobial susceptibility of H. influenzae isolates from children with AOM, elucidate β-lactam and quinolone resistance mechanisms, and determine the molecular epidemiology of resistant strains. We analyzed 182 H. influenzae isolates from the middle ear fluid of children aged ≤3 years with AOM from multiple regions in Japan (February 2022-May 2023). Antimicrobial susceptibility was tested, and β-lactamase genes (blaTEM-1 and blaROB-1) were detected. Sequence analyses of ftsI, encoding PBP3 and quinolone resistance-determining regions were performed to elucidate the resistance mechanisms. Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) was conducted for the ampicillin- and quinolone-low-susceptible strains. Of 182 isolates, 14 (7.7%), 10 (5.5%), 36 (19.8%) and 122 (67.0%) were β-lactamase-producing, β-lactamase-nonproducing ampicillin-resistant (BLNAR), low-BLNAR and β-lactamase-nonproducing ampicillin-susceptible strains, respectively. All 10 BLNAR and 4 β-lactamase-producing isolates exhibited group III PBP3 amino acid substitutions associated with high-level resistance. MLST revealed genetic diversity among BLNAR isolates, whereas 7 (50.0%) β-lactamase-producing isolates belonged to ST103, indicating clonal dissemination. Amino acid substitutions in the quinolone resistance-determining region were detected in six quinolone-low-susceptible strains; these isolates exhibited diverse STs. The β-lactam susceptibility of H. influenzae isolates causing pediatric AOM exhibited an overall improvement. However, an increasing trend in quinolone-low-susceptible strains was observed. Specific clones represented by ST103 were detected among some of the β-lactamase-producing strains, warranting careful monitoring.

title: Natural variation of hypervirulent Klebsiella pathogenicity loci among Taiwan bloodstream isolates
abstract: is a major cause of both nosocomial and community-acquired infections, with hypervirulent (hvKP) strains causing severe disease in healthy individuals. In Southeastern Asia, diabetes mellitus is a recognized risk factor for hvKP-associated pyogenic liver abscesses. hvKP virulence is typically attributed to carriage of a large virulence plasmid encoding siderophore biosynthesis (,) and mucoid regulator (,) genes. Here, we analyzed 50 bloodstream isolates from Taipei, Taiwan, to investigate genomic and phenotypic characteristics of isolates from patients with or without diabetes mellitus. In diabetic patients and patients with liver abscesses, hvKP biomarkers were found in 66% (= 33) and 64% (= 32) of isolates, respectively. While we expected hvKP isolates to be overrepresented in this collection, we observed extensive diversity among hvKP pathogenicity loci, with strains of typical ST23 hvKP lineages carrying incomplete KpVP-1 virulence plasmids. This hvKP biomarker diversity is typically found in classical multidrug-resistant lineages that have acquired portions of the virulence plasmid. Phenotypic assays showed that hvKP biomarkers did not strictly predict hypermucoviscosity, capsule and siderophore production, or survival in serum. Loss ofconsistently eliminated hypermucoviscosity and reduced virulence in a murine pneumonia model, whereas aerobactin loss did not.studies demonstrated variations in virulence that could not be explained solely by differences in the number of hypervirulence-associated loci. These findings highlight the complexity ofpathogenesis and demonstrate that while canonical biomarkers effectively distinguish hvKP from classical, they are insufficient to predict variation in virulence among hvKP strains. Our findings provide insight into the virulence spectrum of strains carrying incomplete plasmid configurations.IMPORTANCEposes a global health threat due to the convergence of antimicrobial resistance and hypervirulence. We identified substantial diversity in virulence plasmid content, including incomplete virulence plasmids within archetypal hvKP lineages, and showed that phenotypic andvirulence traits cannot be fully explained by the presence or absence of individual hypervirulence-associated loci. While canonical biomarkers such asandare widely used to distinguish hypervirulent strains, our analysis demonstrates that no single biomarker is sufficient to reliably predict pathogenic potential and that virulence depends on specific locus combinations and broader context. These findings highlight a critical gap in our understanding of hvKP pathogenesis, underscoring the need for more nuanced frameworks to evaluate virulence. This work has important implications for clinical diagnostics, surveillance, and risk assessment of emergingstrains worldwide.

title: Characterization of clinical isolates of Acinetobacter baumannii and comparative proteomic profiling among strong and weak biofilm formers
abstract: , a critical priority pathogen, is also notable for its biofilm-forming abilities on medical devices like ventilators, catheters, and surgical drain tubes. The biofilm formation causes increased tolerance against antibiotics, making treatment difficult. The clinical isolates ofpresent varied biofilm-forming capacity; hence, understanding the molecular determinants responsible for strong biofilm is crucial. The present study aims to characterize the antibiotic and biofilm-forming profile of 25 clinical isolates ofand compare the proteome profiling of strong and weak biofilm-forming isolates to identify therapeutic targets. We observed= 23 of the isolates as multidrug resistant, and= 13 were forming strong biofilms. Comparative proteomic profiling revealed 42 differentially regulated proteins. In the strong biofilm-forming isolate new lipoprotein A (NLPA), uL16, DNA gyrase B, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and purL were found to be upregulated, highlighting a dynamic reprogramming of cellular functions that promotes biofilm formation, stress adaptation, and immune evasion. In contrast, EF-Tu, ribosome hibernation factors, and T6SS components were downregulated, suggesting a lack of biosynthesis and cellular adaptability. These findings suggest a metabolic downshift and a possible energy conservation mechanism under conditions less favorable for strong biofilm development. Additionally, several uncharacterized proteins were identified, highlighting potential novel factors in biofilm regulation and virulence that warrant further investigation. The proteomics data correlated with qPCR findings, providing support for the unknown regulators of biofilm formation that were identified in this study. Key proteins, such as NLPA, 6,7-dimethyl-8-ribityllumazine synthase, and DNA gyrase B emerged as potential therapeutic targets that may be used for drug discovery. has progressively evolved into a serious cause of both hospital and community-acquired infections. This bacterium's resilience to harsh conditions, bacterial dormancy within biofilms, antibiotic resistance, and survival on inanimate surfaces contribute to its ability to cause chronic, hard-to-eradicate infections. The molecular determinants underlying variations in biofilm-forming capacity among clinical isolates remain insufficiently understood. This study addresses this gap by identifying key molecular adaptations associated with strong biofilm formation. By uncovering pathways linked to biofilm persistence, this work provides valuable insights into bacterial survival strategies and highlights potential avenues for therapeutic intervention. These findings lay the groundwork for the development of new anti-biofilm strategies aimed at improving treatment outcomes and combating antimicrobial resistance.

title: An update on novel and included taxa and revised taxonomic status of bacteria isolated from non-domestic animals described in 2025
abstract: Maintaining an updated list of and analyzing new and revised microbial taxa originating from non-domestic animal species are considered important annual endeavors. As researchers continue to investigate complex microbiota in animal and environmental samples, it is critical that findings are accessible to all with an interest in wildlife animal species. Herein, data concerning novel bacterial taxa and taxonomic revisions of bacteria derived from non-domestic wildlife specimens that were published in peer-reviewed literature and/or accepted during 2025 are summarized and analyzed. While few of the newly identified or accepted bacteria are associated with clinical disease in the host of origin, some are closely related to bacteria that have been implicated in disease or opportunistic infections. Others may contribute valuable information toward future research involving probiotics, antimicrobial resistance, metabolic health, detoxification, and the degradation of toxic materials. Notable bacteria includesp. nov., the first species of psychrotrophic, andsp. nov., which has potential for use as a probiotic in domestic pigs.

title: Whole genome-based characterization of virulence and antimicrobial resistance determinants in clinical Campylobacter jejuni isolates from Minnesota, 2018-2021
abstract: is a leading cause of foodborne gastroenteritis globally and is classified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as a serious public health threat due to increasing resistance to fluoroquinolones and macrolides. This study used whole-genome sequencing to characterize the virulence and antimicrobial resistance profiles of 2,783 clinicalisolates (98.4% stool, 1.2% unknown source, 0.4% blood, and one from rectal swab) collected from Minnesota residents from 2018 through 2021. More than 90% of the isolates had genes related to stress defense (and), cytolethal distending toxin (,, and), and cell adhesion and invasion (,, and). A diverse array of antimicrobial resistance genes were detected, with beta-lactam resistance genes having a particularly high prevalence. Fivepoint mutations associated with quinolone resistance were present in 29% of isolates, with the T861 substitution being the most prevalent. Phenotypically, tetracycline resistance was most common (52.3%), followed by quinolone resistance (30.7%), while resistance to other antimicrobial classes-macrolide (2.4%) and aminoglycoside (1.8%)-was uncommon. To evaluate the correlation between genotypic and phenotypic antimicrobial resistance profiles, the antimicrobial susceptibility testing results from a subset of isolates were compared with genotypic resistance profiles. The results showed a strong overall correlation, particularly for tetracycline and quinolones, though 24 discrepancies were detected. In the majority of discrepancies (= 21), genomic antimicrobial resistance markers were absent in isolates that were phenotypically resistant, suggesting possible unknown resistance mechanisms or limitations in current sequencing analysis methods. The remaining three discrepancies occurred in isolates that had the(O) resistance gene but were susceptible to tetracycline phenotypically. These findings highlight the value of whole-genome sequencing in improving antimicrobial resistance surveillance and understanding virulence-associated factors in, supporting its integration into routine monitoring practices to better manage and understand antimicrobial resistance in foodborne pathogens.IMPORTANCEThis study characterizes the virulence and antimicrobial resistance profiles ofisolates using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data generated through routine foodborne disease surveillance. A subset of isolates was also tested for phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing, allowing us to evaluate resistance patterns and assess genotype-phenotype concordance. This comparison provides important evidence regarding the reliability and limitations of using WGS-detected resistance determinants to predict antimicrobial susceptibility. The 5 years of accumulated surveillance data provide a comprehensive, population-level understanding of circulatingstrains in Minnesota, USA, and establish an important regional baseline for monitoring changes over time. These findings can be compared with national surveillance data to identify geographic similarities and differences and provide a valuable regional context for public health decision-making and antimicrobial stewardship.

title: Sensitivity and specificity of a rapid, point-of-care assay distinguishing bacterial from viral infections in acute care settings
abstract: Differentiating between bacterial and viral infections is essential in the emergency department (ED) to guide appropriate antibiotic treatment. Recent assays, such as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared MeMed BV assay, can help with this distinction. The MeMed BV assay measures three host immune proteins-Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-related apoptosis-induced ligand, Interferon (IFN)-γ-induced protein 10, and C-reactive protein-in blood samples. The results are combined into a score from 0 to 100, where a higher score indicates a higher likelihood of a bacterial infection and a lower score suggests a viral infection or other non-bacterial causes. The study evaluates the feasibility of using the MeMed BV assay-generated score to help clinicians decide whether to order blood cultures in emergency departments, as well as assessing the accuracy of the MeMed BV assay in distinguishing between bacterial and viral infections in ED patients. The assay's performance was also compared with standard biomarker tests and white blood cell (WBC) counts for predicting bacterial infections. This study included 203 illness episodes, of which a total of 108 were associated with bacterial infection (25 had a positive blood culture; 107 had a non-blood sample positive for a bacterial pathogen) and 18 were associated with a viral pathogen. Combined, the MeMed BV assay's "high bacterial likelihood" and "moderate bacterial likelihood" scores yielded a sensitivity and specificity of 87% and 32%, respectively, in correctly identifying any bacterial infection; the scores had a sensitivity and specificity of 95% and 25%, respectively, in correctly identifying bacteremia. The future of differentiating between bacterial and viral infections is moving toward integrated diagnostic methods. To address antibiotic resistance, future diagnostics will leverage host immune response biomarkers, advanced molecular panels, and machine learning techniques. This will enable rapid and accurate results at the point of care. Distinguishing between bacterial and viral infections in healthcare settings can be challenging, as patients often present with similar symptoms and clinical features. In recent years, several new biomarkers have emerged as promising targets for algorithm-based tests designed to differentiate between these types of infections. An increasing number of FDA-approved assays that utilize these biomarkers have entered the market, employing various algorithms. These tests are being used in different clinical settings, such as emergency rooms, to assist clinicians in making accurate diagnoses and prescribing antibiotics appropriately. It is essential for clinicians to correctly order and interpret the results of these assays to fully realize their potential. Our study demonstrates that when such an assay is not used within the FDA-approved context, it does not achieve its full effectiveness.

Enterocin-capped CuZn bimetallic nanoparticles as an innovative strategy to control Salmonella in food safety systems
abstract: Salmonella remains one of the leading causes of foodborne infections worldwide, and the increasing dissemination of antimicrobial resistance has intensified the demand for alternative control strategies applicable to food systems. Bacteriocin-mediated green synthesis has emerged as a promising approach for producing multifunctional nanomaterials with antimicrobial potential. In this study, enterocin-capped copper‑zinc bimetallic nanoparticles (Bio-CuZnNPs) were synthesized through a one-pot green approach using the cell-free supernatant of Enterococcus durans MF5 as both reducing and stabilizing agent. The resulting nanoparticles exhibited spherical morphology, negative surface charge, homogeneous size distribution, and prolonged colloidal stability, indicating effective nanoparticle formation and stabilization by bacteriocin-associated biomolecules. Bio-CuZnNPs showed concentration-dependent antimicrobial activity against Salmonella serovars, with MIC values ranging from 0.5 to 32 mg mLand reductions of up to 6 log CFU mLduring time-kill assays. The nanoparticles also reduced biofilm formation and induced membrane disruption, as confirmed by fluorescence microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and intracellular leakage assays, suggesting that cell envelope damage is a major mechanism associated with bacterial inactivation. In addition, Bio-CuZnNPs exhibited antioxidant activity and maintained antimicrobial efficacy in food-derived test systems, including coconut water and chicken thawing drip. These findings demonstrate that enterocin-mediated CuZn bimetallic nanoparticles combine structural stability with antimicrobial and antioxidant functionalities, supporting their application as multifunctional nanoplatforms for food preservation and mitigation of foodborne pathogens.

title: Prevalence, antimicrobial resistance, and genomic characterization of Streptococcus suis in swine herds of Guangxi, China
abstract: Streptococcus suis is a critical zoonotic pathogen that poses a significant threat to global public health and the swine industry. However, comprehensive epidemiological and genomic data on S. suis in swine herds across southern China remain limited. In this study, we conducted a large-scale surveillance of S. suis isolates from pig farms in Guangxi, China. A total of 210 S. suis isolates were recovered from 2706 throat swabs (7.76%) collected across 12 representative pig farms. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing revealed high resistance rates to erythromycin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and florfenicol, with widespread multidrug resistance (MDR) phenotypes. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) uncovered high diversity in predicted cps types and sequence types (STs). Furthermore, 21 antimicrobial resistance genes associated with seven antimicrobial classes were identified, with resistance genotypes largely correlating with the observed phenotypes. Notably, closely related isolates with minimal single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) variations were identified across geographically distinct farms, indicating the clonal dissemination of specific strains within the region. Global phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that the Guangxi isolates clustered closely with both swine- and human-derived strains from public databases. Taken together, these findings highlight the high prevalence, genetic heterogeneity, and extensive MDR profiles of S. suis in southern China, underscoring the critical need for continuous surveillance and prudent antimicrobial use under a One Health framework.

Chiral antibiotics amplify the phage-associated antibiotic resistome in salinized soil
abstract: Anthropogenic global change is intensifying antibiotic pollution and soil salinization, yet how salinity shapes bacteria-phage interactions to drive the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) under chiral antibiotic pressure remains poorly understood. Using viral metagenomic analyses and laboratory validation, we show that salinity amplifies the enrichment of total and high-risk ARGs along gradients of racemic ofloxacin and its S-enantiomer levofloxacin, concomitant with the parallel accumulation of mobile genetic elements and virulence factors. High-concentration antibiotic treatment in saline soils selected for stress-tolerant, fast-growing antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARBs) carrying abundant prophages and diverse defense systems, thereby promoting tight ARB-phage interactions. Under these dual extreme stresses, lysogenic phages were enriched, enhancing their carriage of ARGs, auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs) that bolster host survival, and antidefense genes via a "piggyback-the-winner" strategy, thereby increasing ARG dissemination potential. Notably, high-concentration levofloxacin exerted stronger selective pressure than ofloxacin, increasing virus-to-host ratios and phage-associated ARG accumulation, as supported by incubation assays. Collectively, our findings support a mechanistic framework in which soil salinization interacts with chiral antibiotic exposure, particularly levofloxacin, to increase phage-associated ARG dissemination potential. This highlights a long-underappreciated, Anthropocene-driven pathway intensifying environmental resistance risks and posing new challenges for the One Health framework.

title: Nanotechnology-based metal, metalloid, and hybrid strategies against urinary tract infections: a narrative review
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) represent a significant and persistent global health concern, especially considering the rise of strains resistant to antibiotics. This review explores the potential of nanotechnology-based approaches to treat these infections. Various nanoparticles, including metallic (such as gold, silver, copper oxide, titanium dioxide and zinc), silica, and carbon-based nanodiamonds, have been investigated for their antimicrobial properties and potential applications in therapeutic management. These nanoparticles exhibit diverse mechanisms of action, including the disruption of bacterial membranes, interference with vital cellular processes, and induction of oxidative stress, resulting in bacterial death. Additionally, nanoparticles can be utilised for targeted drug delivery, preventing bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation, along with enhancing the efficacy of existing antibiotics. Novel strategies such as the green synthesis of nanoparticles and hybrid nanomaterials further expand the scope of treatment. However, most studies to date are preclinical (in vitro and animal-based models), and translation to the clinical landscape remains limited. Therefore, the therapeutic potential of nanotechnology for UTIs should be considered promising, yet preliminary. By harnessing the unique properties of nanomaterials, nanotechnology offers innovative solutions for combating urinary tract infections, potentially reducing reliance on traditional antibiotics and minimising the risk of antimicrobial resistance.
